title: Segmentation and Throttling Strategy Workshop - Peregrine Health
summary: Discovery/demo focusing on org vs project keys, tenant slicing, rate limits and quota policies. Walkthrough of Redwood Console, API examples, and Optimize recommendations. Customer concerned about cost predictability, per-team isolation, and SOC2/KMS requirements. Agreed to run a short pilot with benchmark traffic and share security docs + pricing draft.
topics: Org vs Project key model and routing
API examples and SDK snippets for project keys
Optimize recommendations: batching, caching, quantization suggestions
Security/compliance notes: SSO, KMS, audit logs
action_items: Alex Kim (AE): Share one-pager comparing org-key vs project-key patterns and recommended mapping for Peregrine teams; due 2025-09-18
Samira Patel (SE): Run a 1-hour benchmark using Peregrine sample traffic (200rps with 512 token avg) and send results; due 2025-09-22
Jordan Li (SE): Draft example policy JSON for per-project concurrency and burst tokens and attach to email; due 2025-09-19
Maya Ortiz (Customer Sec): Send list of compliance questions to Redwood security contact; due 2025-09-17
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack (SOC2 report, KMS/HSM integration notes, audit log examples)
Provide pricing draft for Dedicated vs Hosted pilot options
transcript_header:
Meeting header: 2025-09-15 15:30 PDT | Duration: ~52 min | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Ravi Menon (CTO - Peregrine), Laura Chen (SRE), Diego Alvarez (Product), Maya Ortiz (Security)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you all making time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Ravi Menon: Ravi here.
[00:10] Laura Chen: Laura on SRE.
[00:12] Diego Alvarez: Diego, product.
[00:14] Maya Ortiz: Maya from security.
[00:17] Alex Kim: Great. We're going to walk through org vs project keys, how you can slice tenants for billing and throttling, and show the Console + API patterns, then talk about Optimize suggestions for cost. Samira, want to kick off the Console demo?
[00:30] Samira Patel: Yep, jumping in. I'm sharing my screen—okay you should see the Redwood Console dashboard. Top right, you can see org-level quotas, and down here an example project list.
[00:45] Laura Chen: Quick Q, Samira—if we create a project per microservice, will that create separate billing meters? Or is billing still at the org level?
[00:53] Samira Patel: Good question. Billing granularity is flexible. You can charge back at project level by tagging usage; we also show org invoices. So you can do both—most customers do org billing with project-level visibility for cost center chargebacks.
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: How do you recommend mapping teams? We have infra, clinical NLP, and payments—each has different latency/cost sensitivity.
[01:18] Jordan Li: Typical pattern is project keys per dev team or per product capability, and org key for admin/backfill workloads. That lets you apply stricter quotas on noisy teams and keep high-SLA routing for critical services.
[01:31] Ravi Menon: Can we limit concurrency per project? We can't have one team blast all tokens and starve others.
[01:36] Samira Patel: Yes. We demoed concurrency guards earlier—per-project concurrency and per-org fairshare. You can set hard concurrency limits and also a fairshare mode that enforces proportional throughput.
[01:48] Alex Kim: Also support burst tokens—so you can allow short bursts above quota for up to X seconds, with token bucket semantics.
[01:55] Maya Ortiz: On data residency and logs—if we use hosted, do logs leave region? We need audit logs in our EU tenancy.
[02:03] Samira Patel: Hosted API can be region pinned; audit logs and retention policies can be configured to stay in EMEA region. For full control, Dedicated or Private is available.
[02:14] Laura Chen: Ok, demo the API key flow—how do we generate project keys and give them to services?
[02:19] Jordan Li: Back in the Console, create project -> generate key -> you can choose key type: project-scoped or org-key. Project keys are scoped to that project and inherit that project's policy. Org keys bypass project limits but are better for admin tasks.
[02:34] Diego Alvarez: Any SDK examples for enforcement? We want to rotate keys automatically via our secret manager.
[02:39] Samira Patel: We have SDK snippets—here's a curl example and a python snippet. Key rotation is supported; just call the rotate endpoint and update Secret Manager. We also emit key usage metrics back to the Console.
[02:52] Ravi Menon: Let's dig into throttling behavior under overload. If a single project hits the concurrency cap, do we 429 or queue?
[02:59] Jordan Li: You can configure behavior. Options are immediate 429, queue with SLA-based eviction, or graceful degradation to a cheaper model (automatic fallback to a quantized variant).
[03:12] Alex Kim: That's part of our reliability thesis—fallback policies let critical endpoints stay up by degrading model fidelity rather than failing.
[03:19] Laura Chen: Show us Optimize recommendations—how does it tell us when to enable batching vs caching?
[03:25] Samira Patel: In Optimize, we analyze token distribution and access patterns. For repeated prefixes, it proposes KV caching; for many short requests, it recommends batching and gives an expected cost delta and latency impact.
[03:40] Diego Alvarez: Any quick numbers? If we batch 4 requests at 50ms each, what savings?
[03:46] Jordan Li: Depends on model and GPU, but rough rule: batching improves GPU efficiency and can cut per-token cost by ~20-40% for small tokens; Optimize will show model-specific estimates.
[03:58] Maya Ortiz: Security—KMS integration. We need envelope encryption keys in our HSM. Is that supported?
[04:04] Samira Patel: Yes, KMS/HSM integration supported for Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we support customer-managed keys via cloud KMS with wrapped keys; audit logs include key usage.
[04:17] Ravi Menon: What about SSO and RBAC for admin console? We have strict separation of duties.
[04:21] Alex Kim: SSO via SAML/OIDC is supported, with role-based access. You can create fine-grained roles (billing-only, infra-admin, security-audit) and bind them to AD groups.
[04:32] Laura Chen: Do rate limits apply across regions if we split traffic?
[04:36] Samira Patel: Rate limits are global unless you set regional policies. For geo-split workloads we'd suggest per-region orgs or policy rules that tag requests by region.
[04:46] Diego Alvarez: Ok lets talk pilot scope—we want to emulate clinical NLP traffic (variable prompt sizes, spikes during nightly batch processing). Can you support a mix?
[04:55] Jordan Li: Absolutely. For the pilot we'll run two scenarios: steady-state conversational traffic and a nightly spike with long sequence lengths. We'll show concurrency effects, burst handling, and fallback behavior.
[05:06] Alex Kim: We'll also show cost delta if you enable KV caching for common clinical prefixes and if you switch quantized model variants for batch jobs.
[05:14] Ravi Menon: Any gotchas around prefix caching and PHI? We have strict PHI handling for some fields.
[05:20] Samira Patel: Caching is optional and can be disabled for projects handling PHI. Also you can configure caching to strip or redact fields before caching.
[05:30] Maya Ortiz: On audit logs—are they tamper-evident? We need to feed into our SIEM.
[05:35] Jordan Li: Yes logs are integrity-checked and can be forwarded to your SIEM, we support S3/GCS sinks and streaming to Splunk or Datadog. We also include request/response hashes for verification.
[05:47] Laura Chen: Pricing—if we do a Dedicated pool for NLP, can we reserve capacity for spikes? We want predictable latency.
[05:54] Alex Kim: Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and predictable latency; we also have burst credits to handle occasional spikes. Pricing draft will show commit levels and burst credit tiers.
[06:05] Diego Alvarez: Do you offer automatic model variant fallback if Dedicated capacity is exhausted?
[06:09] Samira Patel: Yes, you can configure fallback policies to route to hosted variants or cheaper quantized versions. There's also sticky routing so sticky sessions prefer the same pool until TTL expires.
[06:21] Ravi Menon: How are quotas enforced if we have multiple keys used by the same team? Like service mesh with rotating keys.
[06:27] Jordan Li: Policies can be attached to projects and also to key groups. If keys rotate, the group policy still applies. We support tagging keys and applying policy by tag.
[06:37] Maya Ortiz: Anything in the Console to detect noisy keys automatically? We want alerts.
[06:42] Samira Patel: The Console has anomaly detection rules—set thresholds on token/sec or errors and you get alerts; we also have automatic throttling suggestions.
[06:53] Alex Kim: Let's demo creating a policy—Samira?
[06:55] Samira Patel: Creating policy now—navigating to policies -> create new policy -> set target: project-ClinicalNLP -> concurrency limit 50 -> burst tokens 500 over 60s -> fallbacks: degrade to quantized-8bit -> choose enforcement: queue up to 200 requests -> save.
[07:18] Diego Alvarez: Does the queue preserve ordering? For some of our pipelines ordering matters.
[07:22] Samira Patel: You can choose FIFO or priority queuing; for ordering-sensitive pipelines choose FIFO.
[07:28] Laura Chen: Show logs of enforcement; I want to see an example 429 vs queued event.
[07:33] Samira Patel: Here's the enforcement dashboard—shows hits, rejected, queued, average latency. See example spike from yesterday where a dev test triggered the concurrency cap—requests were queued for ~4s then processed.
[07:48] Ravi Menon: Ok good. On data retention—how long do you keep request bodies in logs?
[07:53] Jordan Li: Default retention 90 days, configurable down to 30 or up to custom enterprise retention. You can also opt to redact bodies.
[08:02] Maya Ortiz: For pilot we'll need an SOC2 addendum and encryption details.
[08:06] Alex Kim: We'll include SOC2 report, encryption architecture, and sample audit log exports in the pack we send.
[08:12] Diego Alvarez: Anything we should watch out for during integration?
[08:15] Samira Patel: Key mapping and tagging up front saves a lot of headaches. We'll provide a recommended project layout and tagging strategy based on your org chart.
[08:25] Ravi Menon: Great. Can you confirm SLAs around Dedicated latency percentiles?
[08:30] Alex Kim: Dedicated SLA guarantees P99 under normal load for the reserved pool; we'll include exact numbers in the pricing/contract.
[08:38] Laura Chen: One more thing—do you provide per-token breakdown by model variant for cost attribution?
[08:42] Jordan Li: Yes, token-level cost breakdown in Console and via API. You can filter by project, key, model, and route.
[08:52] Diego Alvarez: Sounds good. Let's talk timeline—pilot prep and benchmark.
[08:56] Alex Kim: We'll do a kickoff call week of 9/29, Samira will run benchmarks 9/29-10/02 and share results 10/03.
[09:05] Maya Ortiz: Security review window? We need 2 weeks to review SOC2 docs.
[09:09] Alex Kim: We'll send docs today and follow up—happy to book a technical sec review with our security engineer.
[09:16] Ravi Menon: Thanks all. Quick recap and next steps?
[09:20] Alex Kim: Recap: we demoed project key model, concurrency and burst policies, fallback options, Optimize recommendations; next steps are Redwood sends security pack and policy examples, we schedule pilot kickoff 9/29, Redwood runs benchmark and provides pricing draft.
[09:36] Laura Chen: Thanks, helpful.
[09:38] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone—we'll send follow-up with action items and links.
[09:42] (meeting ends, recording stopped)
